title: Moves that help and moves that wait
outcomes: Tells a developing move from a time-wasting move by asking what new work the piece will do
Explains the cost of an early queen trip and of rook-pawn moves by what the opponent does with the time
Recognises when a quiet pawn move is not a waste because nothing can be punished

steps.text: A **developing move** brings a piece to a square where it has work to do. A **wasted move** repeats work already done or does none: moving the same piece again, pushing a rook pawn, taking the queen for an early walk. Wasted moves are not banned. They cost time, and time matters when your opponent can use it to attack.

steps.caption: The game went on like this. Count the developed pieces for each side after each pair of moves.

line.say: A rook-pawn move. No piece comes out.
Black castles. Both knights, the bishop and the king are in play.
At last a bishop comes out.
Black's rook faces the white king along the e-file.

steps.text: A wasted move is mostly punished when the opponent has something to hit. Here White's king is still on e1 and no minor piece (knight or bishop) has moved. Black can open the centre (clear the pawns so the lines to the king open).

line.say: White recaptures. The e-file is open.

steps.title: Does the extra move cost anything?
steps.prompt: A rook-pawn move: predict the cost, then check.
Think of your last game. Name one of your first ten moves that did no new work. What did your opponent do with the extra move?
